title: Your Personal Open-Source Humanoid Robot for $8,999 — JX Mo, K-Scale Labs

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk centers on embodied humanoid robots with multimodal VLA models and realtime physical control loops, matching the embodied-adjacent realtime systems inclusion criterion. Primary domain is robotics and embodied agents; KOS SDK also positions the system as a developer platform for robot programming. Products are in pre-launch with pre-orders open, software launching in 2-3 weeks, and VLA autonomy not yet functional. Accessible full-stack overview from hardware to ML without requiring deep specialization in any single area. Conference presentation with audience Q&A recorded at AI Engineer World's Fair. All claims are first-party statements by a K-Scale founding engineer describing their own products and roadmap.

summary: K-Scale Labs, presented by founding engineer Jingxiang "Jax" Mo, is building fully open-source humanoid robots designed for developers, researchers, and hobbyists. The company open-sources the entire stack—CAD designs, electronics, PCBs, firmware (Rust), software, and ML models—under an MIT license. Their flagship K-Bot is a 4'11" humanoid with a full aluminum body, MIT Cheetah actuators, up to 250 TOPS compute (Jetson Orin/AGX options), and an RL locomotion controller. Priced at $9,000—far below the ~$40k Unitree and ~$60k Tesla Optimus—it targets consumers and developers rather than B2B factory deployments. The Z-Bot, a 1.5-foot humanoid from a hackathon, shares the same software stack. Both feature modular designs for end-effector swaps and component upgrades. The software ecosystem includes KOS, a pip-installable Python/Rust SDK that replaces complex ROS setups, and K-Sim, a digital twin with gRPC interface enabling sim-to-real deployment by changing an IP address. K-Scale avoids ROS because their model-based, policy-driven approach needs few sensors and they prioritize out-of-box simplicity. GPU-accelerated RL training uses MJX, enabling walking policy training in 1-2 hours with ~500 lines of code. The architecture employs a dual-policy system: a high-level VLA controller and a low-level RL whole-body locomotion policy. Currently, capabilities are limited to teleoperation, but as VLA models mature, household tasks like dishwashing and clothes folding are envisioned. The battery provides ~2 hours of walking and supports simultaneous charging via wall power. VR teleoperation uses an RL-based pseudo-IK approach instead of traditional inverse kinematics. The 15-person team leverages ~5,000 Discord members, bimonthly hackathons, open bounties, and is actively hiring. Robots and software launch in 2-3 weeks.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and K-Bot Overview
sections.summary: Jax introduces K-Scale Labs, a 15-person team in Palo Alto building open-source humanoid robots for developers. He motivates the work with physical labor shortage, household, and off-world exploration needs. Introduces the K-Bot: a 4'11" humanoid with full aluminum body, RL locomotion controller, sensor-complete, robust to being kicked, supports VR teleoperation, and available for pre-order with delivery by October.

sections.title: K-Bot Design Philosophy, Open Source, and Modularity
sections.summary: K-Bot designed as simplest possible humanoid at $9,000, roughly robot-arm cost and far below ~$40k Unitree. Entire stack open sourced under MIT license: CAD, electronics, PCB, software, ML models. Modular design enables end-effector swaps (parallel grippers, five-finger hands, third-party grippers) and component upgrades (legs, arms, head) as compute improves. Python/Rust SDK included; supports 5 DOF arms with 7 DOF interchange option; OTA software rollouts weekly.

sections.title: K-Bot Specs and Manufacturing Timeline
sections.summary: K-Bot uses MIT Cheetah actuators, standard components (audio modules, displays, cameras), up to 250 TOPS compute. Project started October last year; moved from 3D-printable K-Scale Stompy prototype to mass manufacturing with a new design reveal coming in two weeks. Pre-orders available at kscale.dev.

sections.title: Z-Bot Introduction
sections.summary: Z-Bot is a 1.5-foot humanoid born from a hackathon project, popular on Twitter and WeChat. Shares same locomotion and software stack as K-Bot, enabling cross-robot app portability. Inspired by Google DeepMind's robot soccer paper. 3D-printed version launched well with ~5,000 Discord members and a few hundred builds. Going to mass manufacturing, also fully open source.

sections.title: ML and Software Stack
sections.summary: Core goal is making K-Bot autonomous via dual policy: high-level VLA controller plus RL whole-body locomotion. Open-sourced GPU-accelerated robot learning library using MJX. Integrating and fine-tuning VLA/generalist policies (Pi Zero, Nvidia GR00T). KOS is a pip-installable Python/Rust framework replacing complex ROS setups. K-Sim digital twin shares gRPC interface; sim-to-real requires only changing IP address. All fully open source.

sections.title: RL Training and Deployment Example
sections.summary: Demonstrates RL training workflow: clone repository, run python training script (~500 lines for walking), train on local GPU via MJX for 1-2 hours, monitor loss and reward in TensorBoard, evaluate in K-Sim, then deploy to real robot by changing IP address. Emphasizes ability to prototype in 1/10th the time of typical training libraries. Development accelerated by open-source community with ~5,000 Discord members and public bounties.

sections.title: Q&A: Battery, Use Cases, ROS, Compute, and Tesla Comparison
sections.summary: Audience Q&A covers battery (slotted pack, ~2 hours walking, can charge via wall plug while running), use cases (consumer focus, not B2B; currently teleoperation only, household tasks like dishwashing pending VLA model improvements), ROS rationale (fewer sensors, model-based policy, bad prior experience with ROS1/ROS2 Foxy/Noetic, wants out-of-box simplicity), compute (Jetson Orin and AGX options), VR teleoperation (pseudo-IK using RL model instead of calculated IK), and Tesla comparison (Optimus more powerful with linear actuators but ~$60k vs K-Bot $9,000; use cases not very different). Team is hiring electrical, firmware, and ML engineers; robots and software launching in 2-3 weeks.
